q: I started throwing around praise like a dog trainer with milk bones.
I’ve since discovered that this is a common belief in education; that the bigger, the more frequent, and the more over-the-top the praise is, the better.
Giving praise privately is more effective than doing it in front of the class.
Small gestures of praise are powerful. Eye contact and a smile from across the room. A note folded over and left waiting on a student’s desk. A hushed, “I knew you could do it.
Praise won’t have meaning to your students if they don’t deserve it. Only offer praise when you notice them doing something that is beyond what is a common classroom expectation.
Praise won’t have its desired effect unless you’re genuinely proud of your student(s). If you don’t feel it in your heart, they won’t feel it either.
When it comes to praising students, more isn’t better. Private, subtle, worthy, and sincere, though, are.

q: Standardized test scores are noticeably higher, year after year, in classrooms with exceptional classroom management. It doesn’t matter who is on the roster.

Over the course of a school year, the difference in quality learning time between a typical classroom and one taught by a classroom management expert can be staggering—amounting to weeks, even months, more in learning time.
In classrooms with few interruptions, the ability of students to concentrate increases tenfold.
This hyper attention to detail is an important test-taking skill that develops over a period of months and is best learned through experience.
The ability to follow directions is a test-taking skill students learn primarily through the practice and repetition of routines and procedures.

t: How To Get The Truth From Untruthful Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/11/13/how-to-get-the-truth-from-untruthful-students/
q: Getting to the truth, though, can be difficult. Backed into a corner, confronted with a report of misbehavior, students are often untruthful.
The why strategy is a way to cut through the deception and get to the truth quickly, so you can get on with the business of teaching.
It's best if the accused (Karla) isn't aware you know anything about the reported incident.
Allow some time to pass before confronting the accused student—at least 30 minutes.
Most teachers will ask a did you question. As in, “Karla, did you push Brian?” But dishonest students are conditioned to lie as soon as the words “did you” begin tumbling out of your mouth.
You, however, are going to ask a why question—which they’re unprepared for. “Hey Karla, why did you push Brian on the way out to recess?
It can turn a potentially frustrating, stressful, and lengthy situation into a 15-second conversation.
x: Waiting about thirty minutes before confronting the accused student increases the element of surprise.

t: Why Students Tattle And What To Do About It
q: There is a reason students tattle. But it has nothing to do with them. They are not the problem. They’re merely doing what they feel like they must do. The problem is with you, their teacher.
Tattling is the result of teachers not fulfilling their most important responsibility: to protect every student’s right to learn and enjoy school without interference.

Your classroom management plan isn't worth the poster it's printed on if you don't follow it. For every rule that is broken, enforce a consequence without a second thought. This simple step removes 90% of tattling.
Frequently remind your class that it’s your job to protect their right to learn and enjoy school. If anyone interferes with that right, you want to know about it.
But tattling has a negative connotation. It discourages students from coming to you with a legitimate problem for fear they’ll be made fun or marginalized for it.
If someone is bothering them, bullying them, or otherwise interfering with learning, they have an obligation to tell you. You must know. It’s your job to know.
x: Discouraging tattling without fixing enforcement leaves students without a legitimate way to report real problems.
